source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME turns mapping into a localist network. Each unit is a hypothesis that one element maps to another. Three soft constraints set the links: structure (isomorphism), semantic similarity, pragmatic importance. The network relaxes to a stable state and the strongest unit per element wins.
numbers: Fixed parameters in all reported runs: decay d=.1, excitation e=.1, inhibition i=-.2. Typical settling well under 100 cycles; never over 220 cycles in any run.
limits: Only fits small hand-written predicate-calculus inputs. Number of units grows with the product of the analog sizes.
agent_relevance: Mapping is a soft multi-constraint problem, not a hard match. For O7 this suggests ranking candidate correspondences by structure, similarity and goal together, with the program doing the counting.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Stability and robustness checks. ACME never lost a correct mapping to a later-rising wrong one. Wide parameter ranges worked.
numbers: Decay .001 to .2 worked equally; excitation .01 to .12 worked, above .12 gave instability; inhibition up to -.9 worked but high inhibition can block recovery from an early wrong mapping. Pragmatic weight best near .3.
limits: Results are for the paper's own example set; no independent stress test on large analogs.
agent_relevance: A mapper that keeps competing hypotheses alive but damps them is stable. Too much inhibition early locks in a bad first guess, which echoes G1 (do not commit or doubt on a schedule).

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Ablation test on the laser/radiation analogy. Deleting every third source proposition or every second target proposition mostly kept the right mappings, except that deleting the predicate 'filament' left the tumor with no positive mapping unit.
numbers: Two ablation runs on the good-constraint laser example; one failure case (lost 'filament').
limits: Qualitative. Single example family.
agent_relevance: Mapping degrades gracefully when facts are missing, but a single missing anchor concept can orphan an element. The agent should flag unmapped elements, not guess.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Convergence problem (Gick and Holyoak 1980; Holyoak and Koh 1987). ACME found the correct mapping in all four lightbulb/radiation versions. Cycles to success did not depend on surface similarity (laser vs ultrasound), and rose slightly in the two poor-constraint versions. In those, the key constraint (do not destroy healthy tissue) had no map at all, which fits the poor transfer in people.
numbers: Holyoak and Koh data quoted in the paper: percent convergence solutions before hint about 69 / 33 / 13 for three versions (one column garbled in the PDF text) and with hint 75 / 60 / 47; ACME cycles to success 3 to 5 for most versions (one value 38 appears; column layout in the extracted text is ambiguous).
limits: Table 5 columns are misaligned in the text extraction, so which cell belongs to which version is uncertain. ACME models mapping only, not retrieval.
agent_relevance: Failure to transfer can come from a missing constraint correspondence, not from failure to retrieve. If the key constraint has no counterpart in the source, the mapper cannot carry the solution.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Gentner and Toupin (1986) children story-acting study simulated. Cycles to success rose slightly from same-object-similar to dissimilar, and sharply in the cross-mapped (similar objects, different roles) condition. In the cross-mapped condition without systematic causal structure, ACME failed to settle on the right mapping.
numbers: Cycles to success listed 3, 4, 38 and 3 for systematic versions, 4 and then no success for nonsystematic versions; exact cell labels are blurred in the extracted table. Similarity weights .06 high, .01 low, .1 identical predicates. Setting i=-.1 or min=-.3 rescued the failure.
limits: Parameter tuning rescued the failure, so the effect depends on settings. ACME shows less same vs different difference than the children did. Younger children (4-6) benefited less from systematicity than 8-10 year olds.
agent_relevance: Cross-mapped surface similarity is the main trap and extra causal structure is what rescues it. The scaffold should state relational roles explicitly when objects look alike but play different roles.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Small human check: can people find an arbitrary attribute isomorphism that ACME finds? Subjects matched five sentences about attributes (smart, tall, timid) to five about other attributes with meaning irrelevant.
numbers: 8 UCLA undergraduates, 3 minutes: 5 gave all six correct correspondences, 2 gave four of six, 1 could not do the task. ACME found all six (network goodness .61, settled by cycle 71).
limits: N=8, informal, no control. Authors used it to defend ACME against the charge of being too powerful.
agent_relevance: Humans can do semantically empty structure mapping, but only for tiny cases. Do not assume an LLM does it reliably for big ones.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Socrates as midwife metaphor (Kittay 1987 analysis) was mapped by ACME with non-isomorphic representations, and a combined bizarre analogy was split into the correct sub-analogies. Missionaries-and-cannibals vs farmer's dilemma homomorphs (Gholson et al. 1988) were also handled with many-to-one mappings.
numbers: Qualitative output tables (best mapping activations about .5 to .9).
limits: The representations were hand coded by the authors, which gives a degrees-of-freedom worry.
agent_relevance: Hand-built representations are where the intelligence sat. For an LLM agent, the restating step (producing the relational form) is the risky step, not the mapping.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME is placed next to SME and Copycat. Copycat also derives the best analogy from parallel competition among hypotheses, but the authors say Copycat and SME constraints explicitly exclude pragmatic considerations while ACME includes them.
numbers: Text comparison only; no head-to-head numbers.
limits: Authors are advocates of ACME; the comparison is theoretical.
agent_relevance: Goal-driven weighting (pragmatics) is the main difference between ACME and structure-only mappers, and matches our rule that goals decide what to map.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME's structural constraint prefers one-to-one mappings via inhibition between competing units. This lets it find isomorphisms without semantic cues, a case where relaxation reaches a global fit from local links alone.
numbers: Table 18 attribute mapping settled by cycle 71 with goodness .61 and activations .54 to .71.
limits: Authors themselves ask whether this is overpowerful relative to people; Hummel and Holyoak (1997) press the point.
agent_relevance: A human-realistic mapper should fail on large isomorphisms; do not treat solver-like success as the reliability target.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: LISA puts access, mapping, inference and schema induction into one architecture. Predicates and objects are distributed semantic patterns bound dynamically by synchrony of firing. Propositions fire one after another in a phase set, so working memory is limited by how many role bindings can fire out of phase.
numbers: Neurophysiology estimate used: a phase set of about 4 to 6 out-of-phase groups (Gray and Singer 1989). Mapping connections can be learned only while both analogs are in working memory.
limits: Simulations are qualitative with hand-set semantic features; small analogs. Model does not learn its own representations in this paper.
agent_relevance: Capacity limits are a feature: the model predicts which analogies need re-representation or external memory. A scaffold can mirror this by mapping a few propositions at a time and writing results to a scratch store.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Access versus mapping difference. Ross (1989) found story-line similarity matters more for retrieval, while object-to-role consistency matters more for mapping. LISA reproduced the reversal, because retrieval uses only pre-existing semantic links, while mapping can build new structural links.
numbers: Qualitative reproduction of Ross four comparisons. Wharton et al. (1994) simulated with eight single-proposition analogs: consistent role assignments retrieved better than cross-mapped, and a singleton study set beat a competition set.
limits: Original Ross numbers are not in the sections I read; LISA does not simulate the familiarity effect (stated as a limit).
agent_relevance: Retrieval and mapping reward different cues. If our agent retrieves analogues by surface similarity it will find cross-mapped traps; the mapping step must check role consistency separately.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Convergence-problem simulation with the radiation problem as driver. Retrieval ordering matched the human ordering (close analog > schema > far analog). Mapping worked for all three sources.
numbers: Mean Luce retrieval indices .43 (close analog Surgeon), .34 (schema), .23 (far analog General). Mapping: all 7 target objects correct for close analog and schema (weights .65 to 1.00); 6 of 7 correct for far analog. Humans given a hint solve at over 80% regardless of source type.
limits: One run per source; no variance across runs reported in the part I read.
agent_relevance: Hints (an explicit instruction to use the source) equalise performance, so an agent should pass the analogue explicitly as a scaffold step, not hope for spontaneous use.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Pragmatic centrality (Spellman and Holyoak 1996, science-fiction planets). People mapped according to the processing goal; LISA reproduced this by firing goal-relevant propositions earlier and more often.
numbers: Human data quoted: economic-goal group mapped Barebrute to Hungerall 43% vs Millpower 35%; military-goal group 29% vs 65%. LISA activations: Econ-hi .63 vs .05 (difference .58); Econ-lo .79 vs .71; Neutral .68 vs .64 (difference .04); Mil-lo difference -.03.
limits: Mapping preference is a graded activation difference, not a hard switch; the human effect is moderate in size.
agent_relevance: The goal should control which relations are examined first. Matches our idea that the problem statement fixes which structure is worth mapping.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Capacity limit prediction: the boys-dogs problem (six correspondences, five propositions per analog) could not be solved by LISA with one proposition or one whole analog in the phase set. It only succeeded when all propositions of both analogs were active together, which needed 10 bindings, beyond the assumed human capacity.
numbers: Failure with 1 proposition and with all 5 propositions of one analog; success only with 10 SPs (role bindings) in the phase set. Mapping was slightly faster when many predicates were similar (all-similar vs one-similar condition).
limits: Prediction rests on the assumed phase-set size; humans can use re-representation or paper.
agent_relevance: Strong design hint: when relational structure is large, split it, re-represent it or write it down. Do not ask one pass to map ten bindings at once.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Development link: LISA ties phase-set size to Halford's relational-complexity levels. Each added slot lets one more role binding be considered in parallel, so bigger working memory means more complex mappings.
numbers: Binary-relation mappings need about 2 to 3 SPs in the phase set (Halford et al. 1994 correspondence); Halford and Wilson (1980) children's mapping experiment is simulated.
limits: Developmental account is explicitly not a definitive explanation, per the authors.
agent_relevance: Links to the working-memory-limit documents in this series. Gives a reason to cap simultaneous bindings per step.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: Hummel and Holyoak criticise ACME as too powerful: it represents all possible local matches at once, which is unrealistic for working memory, and it cannot model learning of new correspondences or effects of mapping order.
numbers: Illustrated by the boys-dogs problem and the unary-predicate isomorphism case from Holyoak and Thagard (1989), which LISA fails within realistic capacity.
limits: Comparison is the LISA authors' argument; human data on boys-dogs not in the sections I read.
agent_relevance: Order of facts presented and capacity matter. Put the goal-central facts first.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1997) The analogical mind
finding: Multiconstraint theory: analogy is guided by similarity, structure and purpose, found by parallel constraint satisfaction. ARCS handles access, ACME mapping, and ACME was extended to inference (Holyoak, Novick, Melz 1994). The models aim to combine symbolic representations with connectionist processing.
numbers: No new numbers; describes the Spellman and Holyoak soap-opera study with plot-extension and mapping tasks.
limits: Review for a general audience; leans on authors' own work.
agent_relevance: Three-way constraint (similarity, structure, goal) is a compact checklist for the mapping step.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in artificial intelligence
finding: Copycat treats analogy as abstract perception. Four parts: concept network (hand built), workspace, many perceptual agents, and a temperature that measures coherence and sets randomness. Representation building and mapping are interleaved with feedback.
numbers: Temperature high early (random, parallel, bottom-up) and falling as a coherent answer forms (more deterministic, serial, top-down). Domain: letter-string problems such as abc -> abd, then ppqqrrss -> ?
limits: Concept network not learned; given source and target, no retrieval; complex ad-hoc parameter tuning; only shown on letter strings.
agent_relevance: Copycat's key idea for our schema: re-represent while mapping, and let the amount of exploration shrink as checks agree. This is a signal-driven version of G1, not a timer.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in artificial intelligence
finding: Mitchell contrasts Copycat's interleaved representation building with the structure-mapping engine, where representations are given first, and calls this a central disagreement. Copycat is neither purely symbolic nor neural.
numbers: Qualitative; conceptual slippage is the abstraction mechanism (letter->group, successor->predecessor).
limits: Review, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Hint for O7: allow a slippage (relax a feature of the source, like direction or role) as an explicit, logged move when a direct mapping fails.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) was compared with UCLA undergraduates on text Digit Matrices (Raven-like), Hofstadter-style letter strings, verbal analogies and Gentner story analogies. GPT-3 matched or beat humans in most settings.
numbers: Digit Matrices (N=40 humans): GPT-3 above humans, generative OR=1.88, p=.005, CI [1.21, 2.91]; multiple choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8. Letter strings (N=57): GPT-3 stronger overall, OR=1.76 for zero-generalisation problems; accuracy falls with number of generalisations in both (GPT-3 OR=.51 per generalisation).
limits: Authors admit training-data contamination cannot be excluded. Tests are synthetic.
agent_relevance: Baseline claim that later work challenged. Do not trust zero-shot analogy ability on altered problems.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogy (Gentner et al. materials, N=54 humans): both GPT-3 and humans chose the story sharing causal relations. In the far (cross-domain) condition GPT-3 was not significant. A preliminary GPT-4 test did better on far analogies.
numbers: Combined p=.0005 (GPT-3), humans t(53)=21.3. Near condition GPT-3 p=.0039; far condition GPT-3 binomial p=.065 versus humans t(53)=16.7, p=9.3e-23. GPT-4 tested on 72 problems through the chat interface: near-perfect near, partial far.
limits: GPT-4 test was informal (web interface, one run). Story set is small.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain mapping with no shared surface is where an LLM is weakest, which is exactly the use case of O7. Test the scaffold on far cases, not near ones.

source: Hodel and West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalisation. Modified letter-string problems (synthetic alphabet, larger letter interval) sharply cut GPT-3 accuracy while humans stayed similar. Authors argue Webb's result may reflect memorised tasks.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy under 0.1 on extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabet with a synthetic alphabet; only remove-redundant and sort stayed in the original range. Counterfactual comprehension checks kept at least 30% of original accuracy for all but one task, so the model could read the change.
limits: Authors' own human sample is small; GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: The model's mapping ability is brittle to surface changes. G3-style held-out tests should include mutated alphabets.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Same conclusion with a bigger design. Humans and GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 solved letter-string analogies on the standard alphabet and on counterfactual alphabets (permuted by 2, 5, 10 or 20 letters, or symbols). Humans stayed high; all models dropped.
numbers: Pooled accuracy table over all alphabets and problem types (1,876 human samples, 6,840 per model): values 0.753, 0.488, 0.350, 0.452 with 95% CIs; the extracted table is garbled, so the assignment of values to humans and the three GPT models is not certain (humans are clearly highest in the figures).
limits: Counterfactual comprehension check shows models can apply successor/predecessor in the new order, so failure is not just misreading. Prompt formats were tuned.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that LLM analogy relies partly on training-data familiarity. A mapping step should be tested on counterfactual relabellings.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas and Mitchell (2024/2025) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near transfer) and symbol (far transfer) alphabets. Children (7-9) and adults did not degrade across alphabets. Every LLM degraded.
numbers: 42 children and 62 adults before exclusions; LLMs Claude-3.5, Gemma-2 27B, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1 405B. Alphabet effect F=29.5 (Claude), 88.2 (Gemma), 55.0 (GPT-4o), 135.0 (Llama), all p<.001; adults and children p=1.0. Item 5 (predecessor + repetition): adults .81, children .38, Claude .20, GPT-4o .39, Llama .44. Item 1 (successor): adults .97, children .85, Claude .90, GPT-4o .92.
limits: Greek given as spelled-out names to LLMs but real symbols to humans. Models were fine on next/previous-letter questions alone but not always the two-step rule.
agent_relevance: Transfer to unfamiliar symbol sets is the gap. If the agent re-represents the problem in a new alphabet it may lose accuracy, so keep the original representation when possible.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière and Pavlick (2024) Semantic structure-mapping in LLM and human analogical reasoning
finding: New tasks map meaningful words to symbol sequences (a length or reversal rule tied to a semantic property). Top LLMs matched humans on the default task but were hurt more by distractors and incoherent semantics on the left side.
numbers: Humans in Defaults about 0.4 to 0.9 match to reference; Only-RHS condition about 0.8 (Claude 3), 0.9 (GPT-4), 0.5 (Llama-405B); GPT-4 not different from humans (p=.824). Random conditions: humans drop about 0.15, Claude 3 about 0.5, GPT-4 about 0.6 and 0.4. Random Finals: models drop 0.5 (Claude 3), 0.8 (GPT-4), 0.4 (Llama), all significantly worse than humans (p<.005).
limits: University student participants; match-to-reference metric. Authors say LLMs give only a how-possibly, not how-actually, account.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant semantic content in the source can pull the LLM off the structure. Strip distractors before mapping.

source: Musker et al. (2024) Semantic structure-mapping in LLM and human analogical reasoning
finding: Related-work claim: Copycat was designed for re-representation but has only been applied to synthetic domains like letter strings; adapting it to open-domain concepts would need major effort. BART (Lu, Wu, Holyoak 2019) learns relations from non-relational input.
numbers: Qualitative statement in the introduction.
limits: Authors' characterisation, not a test.
agent_relevance: Classical mapping models have not been extended to open-world semantics, so the LLM is the only current candidate for that step, with the weaknesses above.

source: Webb, Sinha and Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (ESBN)
finding: A neural net with an external key-value memory that separates abstract keys from content values learned rules that generalised to new entities. This is a learned cousin of LISA-style dynamic binding.
numbers: About 95% or better generalisation on all four tasks, even trained on hundreds of problems with as few as 2 entities (same/different); converged within 100 to 200 updates; other architectures failed in the hardest regime.
limits: Synthetic tasks (same/different, RMTS and others), not natural language. Temporal context normalisation was given to all models; without it generalisation is worse.
agent_relevance: Evidence that binding by variable and slot gives rule transfer. For an LLM scaffold: write explicit role variables (X, Y) in a scratch store.
